Proof attempt:
Step 1: By Hall's Marriage Theorem, G has a matching saturating A if and only if for all subsets S of A, |N(S)| >= |S|. (Justified)
Step 2: Let S be an arbitrary subset of A. We want to show |N(S)| >= |S|. (Justified)
Step 3: Let E(S, N(S)) be the number of edges between S and N(S). Since every vertex in A has degree at least 1, E(S, N(S)) >= |S|. (Justified)
Step 4: Since every vertex in B has degree at most 2, the vertices in N(S) are incident to at most 2|N(S)| edges. (Justified)
Step 5: Thus, E(S, N(S)) <= 2|N(S)|. (Justified)
Step 6: Combining Step 3 and Step 5 yields |S| <= 2|N(S)|. (Justified)
Step 7: From |S| <= 2|N(S)|, it follows that |S| <= |N(S)|. (Invalid)

Step 7 is invalid because |S| <= 2|N(S)| does not imply |S| <= |N(S)|. For example, if |S|=2 and |N(S)|=1, the inequality holds but |S| <= |N(S)| is false. This reflects the fact that the original statement is false.
